Hi Michael,

I'm Jon Clark, and I'm interested in your 2016 Nissan Altima. Before we go any further, I have to be upfront: your asking price of $12,600 is above even the top of the KBB private-party range ($10,990–$12,540), while the estimated fair value sits at $11,765. 

I'm prepared to offer **$10,800**, but that number also depends heavily on the car's mechanical history. Can you provide maintenance records and confirm whether there are any existing mechanical issues, overdue repairs, or accident history I should know about?

Looking forward to hearing the details.

— Jon

Michael,

Hold on. Before I could even respond to your maintenance list, I received independent confirmation that this Altima has a known, significant transmission failure—specifically CVT issues—that you are actively instructing your agent to conceal. Representing the car as having “no existing mechanical issues” and being in “excellent shape” while knowingly hiding a major mechanical defect is material misrepresentation, not a pricing disagreement.

Under a fact-based valuation, the KBB private-party figure for a healthy example is $11,765. A CVT transmission replacement on this model runs roughly $3,500–$4,000, which would adjust the car’s real value to around $8,000. But I’m not going to make a reduced offer. I don’t purchase vehicles from sellers who deliberately conceal material defects.
